newsitem.title: SPAIN: Europe not in shape for euro yet, Issing says.
newsitem.headline: Europe not in shape for euro yet, Issing says.

text.p: Europe has yet to shape up flaccid budgets sufficiently and its overall fitness for the single currency launch remains questionable, Bundesbank board member Otmar Issing said on Thursday.

Issing, speaking to bankers at a seminar in this northern Spanish town, said two key reports last week on economic convergence left open the question of whether Europe had exerted itself enough in preparing for the euro launch in 1999.
"In the light of these reports, the findings on the progress on convergence made so far are ambivalent," said Issing, also the Bundesbank chief economist.

The European Commission and the European Monetary Institute each published reports on how nations were faring on fulfilling strict criteria on inflation, long-term interest rates, deficit, debt and foreign exchange stability.
Candidates aiming to be founding euro members had clearly not made enough progress in the crucial area of public finances, on which the eventual selection process will hinge, Issing said.

"It is true that, on the one hand, inflation rates have been significantly reduced and that nominal long-term interest rates of most countries have converged distinctly as a result. On the other hand, consolidation of public finance is still largely unsatisfactory," Issing said.
Almost every EU member significantly exceeded the qualifying thresholds of three percent of gross domestic product for the current budget deficit and of sixty percent for government debt.
"The group of candidates selected for monetary union therefore depends decisively on further consolidation in the area of public finance," Issing said.
He added that this explained why criticism of strict adherence to the budget criteria was getting ever more strident.
"It is hardly surprising in such a situation that criticism of the sense and purpose of strictly adhering to the budget criteria is getting louder," Issing said.
He took a swipe at budgetary "manipulation," arguing that compliance must be real if austere budget policy is to be sustained.

"Dressing up the figures on budget deficits or government debt by imaginative manipulation -- even if, in individual cases, this is compatible, in a formal sense, with the guidelines on the national accounts --is certainly not consistent with the spirit of the relevant provisions in the Maastricht Treaty," Issing said.
Issing criticised, for example, France's move to use Telecom pension funds to help narrow its budget for 1997.
"That is not a case that should be taken as an example," Issing said.
